| Meeting | Session B leaves you with |
|:---|:---|
| **1** &nbsp;Introductions | Three things your group would like to explore, and who would care about each |
| **2** &nbsp;Theory and causality | Your team's ground rules, and the first causal graph of your own question — treatment, outcome, the back door you must close, and the variable you must not touch |
| **3** &nbsp;Finding the question | Your team's question slate — three candidate questions, each labelled with an archetype and run through the four filters, with one killed on the record |
| **4** &nbsp;Ethics and access | Your project's ethics-and-access checklist — every gate it trips, who signs, and the date each one has to start |
| **5** &nbsp;Coding tools and AI | Your candidate dataset interrogated — or, if you do not hold one yet, the named access route and plan B for getting it |
| **6** &nbsp;Models and uncertainty | The overclaim your own project is most at risk of making |
| **7** &nbsp;Model failures | The one threat your design must survive — its direction, and whether controls can close it |
| **8** &nbsp;Research designs I | Whether an experiment, instrument or discontinuity is open to you |
| **9** &nbsp;Research designs II | Your design defended in public, plus the attack that landed — the identification section and the limitation |
| **10** &nbsp;Writing | Your problem statement, as an outline somebody outside your team could follow |
| **11** &nbsp;Figures | Your project's key figure, drawn twice — as you expect it to look, and as it looks if you are wrong |
| **12** &nbsp;Speaking | Your final-presentation deck, rehearsed and attacked — plus the gap between the claim you made and the claim the room heard |
| **14** &nbsp;The pitch | Your plan, pitched — and what your team owes AEM 6992 over the break |
